pr.title: Plan giving each project page a summary's sidebar
pr.head: e25be77a4a7e997207a3a3155f861ef2575d82f7

summary: Projector's site has two kinds of page that show the same pull requests in different ways. A summary page describes one pull request and has a boxed sidebar at its left that lists the pull request's whole stack, the chain of dependent pull requests it belongs to, one row per pull request. A project page renders one plan from docs/projects/ and lists the reviews that link to it as one flat line in its page head, such as Reviews #212 Incremental review plan.

The flat line shows no stacks, leaves out layers that have no summary, and scrolls away with the page head. A project with supplemental files also shows a separate tree of pages in a plain column at the window's left edge.
This pull request adds the plan project-page-nav, at status ready and priority next. It changes no code. The plan gives every page of a project the summary page's sidebar, drawn by the same code:

1. The stacks are every stack that holds a segment of this project, newest first. A segment is a run of layers in one stack that carry the same project. Each stack shows whole, as a summary's sidebar shows it, with every segment's header, merged and closed layers included. This project's headers are current on its readme, and other projects' headers link to their pages.
  2. The pages are the project's supplemental files and nested projects, which move out of the tree column.
  3. The footer row keeps Projector's credit, and its history icon links to the plan's commits on GitHub.

The page takes the summary page's layout whole: a title row across the top, drawn by the same titleRowHtml helper a summary uses, holds the breadcrumbs, the badges, View on GitHub, and the plan's title, and the sidebar and the plan sit side by side beneath it. The plan's own first <h1> leaves the body, so the title shows once, and the review line goes. In the build, each project's stacks in site.json, a list of stacks that are each a list of segments, replaces its reviews.

The plan depends on stack-header (#216, merged as a plan, not yet implemented) and on its amendment in #226, still in review. Under the amendment, each pull request records one project or none, and the build splits each stack into segments, each with a header and its members. This plan reuses those segments, adds no request to GitHub, and takes the names the amendment settles. It leaves a list of the plan's sections in the sidebar to a follow-up plan.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Stack: pull requests that build on one another, listed from the bottom layer up. A pull request alone is a stack of one.
  • Segment: a run of layers in one stack that carry the same project, under one header. A layer that names no project joins the segment beneath it.
  • Header: what stack-header puts above a segment, either a project, linked to its page, or a plain-text title for a stack that names no project.
  • Entry: one pull request's record in build_summaries, in the order the Reviews index lists them.
  • Current header: a header that names the page you are on, drawn highlighted and not as a link.
  • Tree column: today's column of a project's pages, fixed to the window's left edge at 240 pixels.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html:
• The first review, at 206c7fc, found that the project sidebar would start about 70 pixels higher than a summary's. 6c508f7 fixed it by giving the project page a summary's title row.
  • Two reviews found prose lines past the plan's 80 columns, which 9765e89 and eb396fa rewrapped.
  • e25be77 moves the sidebar onto segments from #226. Its review is clean, with suggestions to name stackSegmentsHtml, to restate the segment rule as #226 words it, and to place #218's banner now that #218 has merged.

groups.title: The project-page-nav plan
groups.kicker: One shared sidebar for project pages and summary pages, and the site.json field that feeds it
intro: The plan has seven numbered sections. Section 1 shows what a project page lists today. Section 2 is the design: the page layout (2.2), what the sidebar shows (2.3), the build change (2.4), the shared renderer and its style rules (2.5), narrow screens and accessibility (2.6), and the interface a proposed project's page needs (2.7). Section 3 gives the reasons and the rejected alternatives, and section 4 lists the tests.

Three decisions carry the design. The project page takes the summary page's layout rather than drawing the sidebar inside the existing tree column. A stack shows whole on the page of every project that heads one of its segments, so it looks the same there as in each member's own sidebar. And stacks stores segments of pull request numbers, so each row takes its title from site.json's reviews and every title is written once.

checks.text: The plan is at ready, which claims it can be implemented without further questions. It is implemented after stack-header and its amendment in #226, whose segments, find_stacks, and stackHeaderHtml it reads.

Two questions are left to a follow-up plan, project-page-sections (#222, a draft stacked on this pull request): a list of the plan's sections in the sidebar, and how a nested project's sidebar reaches its sibling projects. Until then, a nested project's page reaches its parent through the breadcrumbs.

proposed-projects (#218) has merged. It gives a proposed project an ordinary record and resolves stack headers against proposed projects, which meets both conditions in § 2.7. Its banner sits above the status badges, which this plan moves into the title row.

files.note: The new plan, at status ready and priority next.

checks.text: Section 2.2: with a title row and a sidebar, frame in site/src/site.ts draws the summary page's layout. A .wrap opens with header.top, followed by a .layout grid of a 250-pixel sidebar and a content column, under a site bar that scrolls away.

A summary's sidebar starts below its title row, because renderPage draws header.top inside .wrap and above .layout. The project page now does the same. Checked by reading renderPage and both stylesheets on main.

The title row's heading matches the <h1> that this step removes. title_from_text in src/projector/core.py, which page_title also calls, takes the first line that starts with # and a space. Checked by reading both functions.

Section 2.3: each stack draws whole. A header that names this project is current on its readme, and a link on a supplemental page. A header that names another project links to that project. Only the first current header carries aria-current.

Every page of a stack carries the same segments under #226, and each entry's stack is its index group's first number, or None for a group of one. So project_stacks takes each stack once and files it under every project its headers name. Checked against #226's § 8.2 and build_summaries on main.
Section 2.4: stacks holds each stack as its segments, newest stack first. A stack that spans two projects is written under each, and a stack whose only header is a title is under none.

Section 2.5: sideNavHtml draws both sidebars, one .stackgroup per stack and a header with its rows per segment. #226 adds stackSegmentsHtml for the same part of a summary's sidebar, which this plan does not name yet.

The scoping problem is real. site.css writes the tree column as .sitemain .side, which also matches a sidebar aside.side inside main, and site.css loads after summary.css in home_page. Checked by reading both stylesheets and the page shell.
Section 2.7 names what a proposed project's page needs: a project record, and stack headers that carry its name. Merged #218 provides both.
The 42-pixel figure holds. Every element is border-box, so the 240-pixel tree column with 16-pixel padding leaves 208 pixels, against the summary sidebar's 250-pixel grid column.

Section 3: a stack shows whole on the page of every project it carries out. The rejected options were showing only this project's segments, and showing a stack only under its bottom segment's project.

Section 4 writes a stack as its segments, such as alpha/beta 9 · alpha 10. The rows cover a stack that spans two projects, a project that recurs in one stack, and exactly one aria-current in every page test.
